newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FEATURE-ECONOMY STABILISES, BUT BULGARIANS STILL STRUGGLE.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-ECONOMY STABILISES, BUT BULGARIANS STILL STRUGGLE.

text.p: Bulgarians are no longer grabbing headlines with queues for bread, fuel or cash handouts, but the vast majority still face a quiet daily struggle to survive.
Boika Blagoeva, a head of department at Sofia's Alexandrova teaching hospital, says the effects of months of hardship are starting to show in her patients.

"Half of them have high blood pressure from the stress they have to cope with every day and from bad nutrition," she said. "And something else I have noticed -- the age of heart attack and stroke patients has fallen sharply."

Blagoeva is scarcely better off herself. Although well qualified and working in a modern hospital, she earns a state salary of 60,000 levs ($40) a month which has failed to keep pace with the collapse of the lev.
Her husband, also a doctor, brings home a similar wage, and they struggle to support two student daughters, one living at home and one outside Sofia.
"I can't say myself how we're getting by," she said. "With such a salary we can buy food, but nothing else."
The hospital has had to introduce charges for consultations and tests which were previously free. A typical set of tests for a stomach complaint could cost 11,000 levs, she said.
"When I write a prescription, I can't be sure that the patient will buy the medicines. Some patients have told me directly that they cannot buy them," Blagoeva said.

A recent government report said real incomes in 1996 had fallen by some 65 percent since 1990. "The consumption of a considerable part of the population has shrunk to around the level of biological survival," it said.
The interim cabinet which took office in February tackled the worst of the crisis, restoring fuel and grain supplies and halting the collapse of the lev.
IMF PACKAGE APPROVED, MORE AID PROMISED

The International Monetary Fund last week approved a $657 million funding package, and lenders including the European Union, the Group of 24 industrialised countries and the World Bank have pledged a similar sum.
"Now that the IMF has approved the agreement with Bulgaria the real work is starting and the next couple of months will be crucial," said Economic Policy Minister Krassimir Angarski.
Bulgaria's interim cabinet has agreed to tough conditions, including the introduction of a fixed exchange rate regime in June, to restore confidence in the collapsing lev currency.
Another priority is a rescheduling agreement with the Paris Club of government creditors. Payments on Bulgaria's $9.65 billion debt amount to $1 billion this year.

All political parties have declared their support for the reform programme, though the Bulgarian Socialist Party, which polls predict will form the main opposition in the new parliament after Saturday's elections, has criticised what it says is a lack of transparency over the negotiations.

Under a currency board, levs in circulation must be strictly matched to foreign currency reserves, putting strict limits on monetary policy. The lev will be effectively pegged to either the dollar or the mark, at around the market rate at the time of introduction.

The election campaign of the Union of Democratic Forces, expected to win a majority in the new parliament, emphasises the positive aspect of the reforms, but government spending cuts and closures of loss-making state companies will create new problems.

Unemployment hit 13.7 percent of the workforce in February and is set to rise further. The National Labour Exchange says another 160,000 workers are expected to be laid off by the end of the year, some 100,000 from industrial enterprises and around 58,000 from the public sector.

The World Bank is helping with severance payments and grants to help some of those thrown out of work to set up small businesses, but Social Welfare Minister Ivan Neikov said the sudden poverty was toughest on people like Blagoeva.
"For many people it requires a major adjustment as they have a good education and qualifications but suddenly they have found themselves living in misery," he said. REUTER
